passages.t: The law read from daybreak to noon
passages.happening:
‘At that time all the people gathered together in the square before the Water Gate, and they asked Ezra the scribe to bring out the Book of the Law of Moses, which the LORD had commanded for Israel’ (verse 1).

‘On the first day of the seventh month, Ezra the priest brought the Law before the assembly of men and women and all who could listen and understand’ (verse 2). He reads it aloud from daybreak until noon, ‘And all the people listened attentively to the Book of the Law’ (verse 3).

Ezra stands on a high wooden platform built for the day, with leaders beside him. When he opens the book, all the people stand up. He praises the LORD, the great God, and the people lift their hands and answer amen, twice over, and they bow with their faces to the ground (verse 6). Levites move among the people, teaching them as they stand in their places. ‘So they read from the Book of the Law of God, explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The wall is finished, and the story turns from stones to Scripture. Chapters 8 to 10 are the spiritual center of the book: the law is read and understood, the people confess their sins, and they bind themselves to keep it.

If these chapters follow straight on from the wall's completion on the twenty-fifth of Elul, the first day of the seventh month came only days later, in the autumn of about 445 BC. The seventh month was the greatest festival month of Israel's year. Its first day was a day of rest marked by trumpet blasts, the tenth was the Day of Atonement, and from the fifteenth came the Feast of Tabernacles.

The people ask for the book. Ezra does not have to call them. And the assembly meets in the open square by the Water Gate, near the Gihon spring on the east side of the city, not in the temple courts, so that men, women and all who could understand could gather together.

Standing when the scroll was opened was a sign of respect. The names of the leaders beside Ezra show a shared act of the whole leadership, not one man's performance.

The word in verse 8 translated explaining it may mean reading clearly, section by section, or it may mean translating. Many of the returned exiles spoke Aramaic, the common language of the Persian empire, and some Jewish tradition saw here the beginning of spoken Aramaic translations of Scripture. Either way, the goal was understanding.
passages.later: The law itself commanded such a reading: ‘you are to read this law in the hearing of all Israel’ (Deuteronomy 31:11). And Paul asked Timothy to keep the same practice in the church: ‘devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching’ (1 Timothy 4:13).
passages.hard:
What did the Levites do in verse 8: explain the reading, or translate it?

The Hebrew word can mean making something clear, reading section by section with pauses, or it can mean translating. Those who favor translation point out that many returned exiles spoke Aramaic, the common language of the empire, and that later Jewish practice set a translator beside the reader of the law. Those who favor explanation note that the verse goes on to speak of giving insight, so that the people could understand.

Both readings agree on the point of the verse. The law was not only to be heard but understood, and the leaders took trouble to make sure that ordinary people could follow it.
passages.asks: The people asked for the book, stood when it was opened, and listened for six hours. Ask how hungry you are to hear God's word, and what it would take to listen like that. And ask who helps you understand what you read, and whom you could help.

passages.happening:
As they hear the words of the law, the people weep. Nehemiah the governor, Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites tell them, “This day is holy to the LORD your God. Do not mourn or weep” (verse 9).

Nehemiah says, “Go and eat what is rich, drink what is sweet, and send out portions to those who have nothing prepared, since today is holy to our Lord. Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength” (verse 10). The Levites calm the people: “Be still, since today is holy. Do not grieve” (verse 11).

‘Then all the people began to eat and drink, to send out portions, and to rejoice greatly, because they understood the words that had been made known to them’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The people weep because the law shows them how far they have fallen short. The leaders do not deny their sin, but they turn this holy day toward joy. The confession will come in its proper place, in chapter 9.

Holiness here is shown not by gloom but by feasting, generosity and rest. The holy God is also the giver of good things. And the feast is not only for those who can afford it. Portions are sent to those who have nothing prepared, as the law had always wanted the poor to share in the feasts.

The verb to understand, bin, runs through the chapter: those who could understand, the Levites helping them understand, and the people rejoicing because they understood. God's word is meant to be grasped, not only heard, and understanding it brings joy.
passages.later: The law had made room at the feasts for those with nothing: ‘And you shall rejoice in your feast’ (Deuteronomy 16:14), with sons and daughters, servants, the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widows.
passages.asks: The people wept at what the law showed them, and they were told to feast and to share. Ask whether you let God's word bring you to grief and then to joy, or only to one of them. And ask who has nothing prepared, and how you might send them a portion.

passages.happening:
On the second day, the heads of the families, with the priests and Levites, gather around Ezra to study the words of the law. ‘And they found written in the Law, which the LORD had commanded through Moses, that the Israelites were to dwell in booths during the feast of the seventh month’ (verse 14).

So they send word through the towns and Jerusalem: go out to the hills and bring back branches of olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm and other leafy trees, to make booths, ‘as it is written’ (verse 15). The people build booths on their rooftops, in their courtyards, in the courts of the house of God, and in the squares by the Water Gate and the Gate of Ephraim.

‘The whole assembly who had returned from exile made booths and lived in them. From the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day, the Israelites had not celebrated like this. And there was great rejoicing’ (verse 17). Day after day Ezra reads from the law, and they keep the feast for seven days, with an assembly on the eighth (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The scene narrows to the leaders studying the law and then widens again to the whole people building booths. They obey as they discover.

During the Feast of Tabernacles, Israelites lived in temporary shelters of branches, to remember that God had made them live in booths when he brought them out of Egypt. For returned exiles, who knew what it was to have no settled home, the sign would have had fresh meaning.

The law also commanded that it be read to all the people at this feast every seventh year. Ezra reads from it every day of the feast.
passages.later: The law of the feast: ‘You are to dwell in booths for seven days’ (Leviticus 23:42). And the law of the reading: ‘At the end of every seven years, at the appointed time in the year of remission of debt, during the Feast of Tabernacles’ (Deuteronomy 31:10), the law was to be read to all Israel.
passages.hard:
If the Israelites had not kept the feast like this since Joshua's day, what about the earlier celebrations the Bible mentions?

Verse 17 says that from the days of Joshua the Israelites had not celebrated like this. Yet Ezra 3:4 records the returned exiles keeping the Feast of Tabernacles, and the books of Kings and Chronicles describe a great festival at the dedication of Solomon's temple in the seventh month.

Most interpreters conclude that the statement is about the manner and the scope of the celebration, not about whether the feast was kept at all. This time the whole community actually lived in booths, built on rooftops, in courtyards and in public squares, as the law described, and with a joy tied to rediscovering the law. Chronicles says similar things about the Passovers of Hezekiah and Josiah, which were unlike anything before them in their character, though they were not the first ever kept.
passages.asks: The people found a command in the law and obeyed it the same week. Ask what you have found in Scripture that you have not yet acted on. And ask what reminds you, as the booths reminded Israel, that God has carried you through a wilderness.
